summary: Georgia runs one of the world's most liberal entry regimes: citizens of around 95 countries — including the US, UK, EU, Ukraine, Turkey and Russia — can stay visa-free for a full year, while most other nationalities either qualify via a valid Schengen, US or UK visa or residence permit, or apply for a cheap short-stay eVisa at evisa.gov.ge.

Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Georgia

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a valid visa or residence permit from the US, the UK, the EU/Schengen area or several other listed countries may enter Georgia visa-free for 90 days.

source.name: Geoconsul — visa-free regime and visa information

conditionalWaivers.text: Holders of a GCC residence permit (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain or Oman) can enter Georgia visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period — since April 2025 the permit must be valid for at least 12 more months for many nationalities.

fee.notes: Approximately USD 25 in total (visa fee plus service fee — roughly GEL 88 equivalent), paid online by card.

source.name: Georgia e-VISA Portal — Ministry of Foreign Affairs

passportValidity.text: Your travel document must be valid for the whole intended stay; eVisa applicants should carry a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond the planned entry date.

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement (it is recommended for eVisa applications and mountain activities) — medical care outside Tbilisi is limited and evacuation coverage is worth having for trekking and skiing.

onwardTicket.text: Onward tickets are rarely checked for visa-free travelers, though airlines and border officers may ask about the purpose and length of your stay.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; border officers may ask visitors to show sufficient means for their stay.

currencyLimits.text: Cash and securities worth more than GEL 30,000 (or the foreign-currency equivalent) must be declared on entry.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Georgia

notes: Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 4 liters of alcoholic beverages per adult.
Medicines for personal use are fine in reasonable quantities; strong opioid painkillers require documentation.

payments.text: Cards and contactless are accepted almost everywhere in Tbilisi, Batumi and Kutaisi, including the metro. Carry cash (lari) for rural guesthouses, mountain regions, marshrutka minibuses and small markets.

safety.text: Georgia is generally safe with low violent crime; visitors mainly face petty scams and aggressive driving. Avoid the Russian-occupied regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia and their boundary lines, where consular help is unavailable.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Georgia travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–June and September–October bring mild weather for Tbilisi, wine country and the Caucasus trails; September–October also coincides with the rtveli grape harvest. High mountain passes are open roughly June to October.

idp.text: Georgia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3); Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Georgia is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Georgia yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties

tips.text: Never enter Abkhazia or South Ossetia from the Russian side — entering Georgia through these occupied regions is a criminal offense under Georgian law and can mean fines or imprisonment when you cross into government-controlled territory. Approaching the boundary lines is also risky.

Georgia is the world's oldest wine region — 8,000 vintages of qvevri (clay-vessel) winemaking, UNESCO-listed. Base yourself in Sighnaghi or Telavi for the Kakheti wine route, and try amber (skin-contact) wines at family wineries.

Mountain roads to Kazbegi, Svaneti and especially Tusheti (the Abano Pass) are narrow, unpaved in stretches and weather-dependent. Hire a local 4x4 driver rather than self-driving, and expect closures outside June–October.
Tap water is safe to drink in Tbilisi and most towns. It comes from mountain sources; in remote villages or after heavy rain, bottled water is a sensible fallback.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Georgia?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can enter Georgia visa-free and remain for a full year (365 days). No registration, no arrival card. To reset the clock, travelers simply exit and re-enter, though very frequent resets can draw questions at the border.

faq.question: How long can I really stay in Georgia visa-free?
faq.answer: A full 365 days per entry for the roughly 95 nationalities on the visa-free list, including the US, UK, all EU states, Canada, Australia, Japan, Ukraine, Turkey and Russia. It is one of the most generous visa-free allowances in the world, which is why Georgia is popular with remote workers.

faq.question: Do Indian citizens need a visa for Georgia, and how much is it?
faq.answer: Yes, unless they hold a valid visa or residence permit from the US, UK, EU/Schengen or GCC states — in that case they enter visa-free for 90 days. Otherwise the short-stay eVisa at evisa.gov.ge costs about USD 25 including the service fee and allows a 30-day stay within a 120-day window.

faq.question: Can I enter Georgia with a Schengen, US or UK visa?
faq.answer: Yes. Holders of a valid visa or residence permit issued by the US, UK, EU/Schengen states, GCC countries and several others can enter Georgia without a Georgian visa and stay for 90 days within any 180-day period — a route widely used by travelers from India, the Philippines and Pakistan.

faq.question: Can I visit Abkhazia or South Ossetia from Georgia?
faq.answer: Both regions are Russian-occupied and outside Georgian government control; most governments advise against all travel there and consular help is unavailable. Crucially, entering them from the Russian side is a criminal offense under Georgian law — if you later cross into Georgia proper you risk fines or imprisonment.
